categories.name: Radon monitors & test kits
categories.short: Continuous digital monitors and lab-analyzed kits for the one test every Canadian home needs.
categories.why: A lab-analyzed long-term kit is what Health Canada's protocol is built on — it produces the defensible 3-month average you make decisions with. A continuous digital monitor complements it: you watch levels move with seasons and renovations, and you verify a mitigation system keeps working year after year.

picks.name: Alpha-track long-term kit (C-NRPP-listed)
picks.why: A passive detector you place for 3+ winter months and mail to an accredited lab — the exact test Health Canada's guidance is written around, and the cheapest defensible answer.
picks.q: radon test kit long term alpha track Canada

picks.name: Airthings Corentium Home 2
picks.why: Battery-powered digital monitor with day/week/long-term averages on the display — easy to move room to room, and the long-term number is the one that matters.

picks.name: Ecosense RadonEye
picks.why: The consumer monitor with the most sensitive readout — reacts in hours rather than days, which makes it the tool for watching what air-sealing or a new mitigation fan actually did.

notes: Decisions follow the 3-month average, never a daily readout — radon swings with weather.
After mitigation, a continuous monitor is the cheap insurance that the fan is still doing its job.
Levels above 200 Bq/m³? That's a C-NRPP mitigation quote, not a bigger monitor.

categories.name: Indoor air quality monitors
categories.short: PM2.5, CO₂, and humidity numbers for the air you actually breathe — smoke days included.
categories.why: You can't manage what you don't measure. A particle (PM2.5) reading tells you when wildfire smoke has made it indoors and whether the purifier is keeping up; CO₂ tells you whether the house is under-ventilated for the people in it — the same question the audit's ventilation assessment answers with instruments.

picks.name: Airthings View Plus
picks.why: Radon, PM2.5, CO₂, humidity, VOCs, and pressure in one wall-mounted display — the single-device answer for a whole-home baseline.
picks.q: Airthings View Plus air quality monitor

picks.name: Aranet4 Home
picks.why: The reference consumer CO₂ monitor — e-ink display, years on a battery, NDIR sensor. Under ~800 ppm your ventilation is keeping up; sustained higher numbers make the case for an HRV.

picks.name: Amazon Smart Air Quality Monitor
picks.why: PM2.5, VOC, humidity and temperature for the price of a dinner out — enough to see smoke infiltration and check purifier placement, minus the CO₂ sensor.

notes: On wildfire-smoke days, indoor PM2.5 below ~12 µg/m³ is the target — if the number climbs when the purifier is running, it's undersized or mis-placed.
CO₂ is a proxy for ventilation, not a pollutant at household levels — it tells you when to ventilate and when an HRV would pay off.
Humidity readings on these double as your mould early-warning: winter target roughly 30–50%.

categories.name: Air purifiers (HEPA)
categories.short: True-HEPA units sized to the room — the practical defence on smoke days and the ally during dusty renovations.
categories.why: A properly sized true-HEPA purifier is the fastest air-quality win money can buy: it strips wildfire-smoke particles, renovation dust, and allergens from the room you actually live in. It treats symptoms, not causes — mould needs its moisture source fixed and radon needs mitigation — but on a smoke day or mid-renovation, nothing else works as fast.

picks.name: Coway AP-1512HH Mighty
picks.why: The default recommendation in this category for a decade — true HEPA, quiet, frugal on power, filters that don't cost a fortune. Right-sized for bedrooms and offices to ~35 m².

picks.name: Winix 5500-2
picks.why: True HEPA plus a real washable carbon filter — the combination that handles wildfire-smoke smell, not just the particles. Regularly the best value per unit of clean air delivered.

picks.name: Levoit Core 600S
picks.why: Moves enough air for open-plan main floors and basements (~70 m²) with app control and an onboard particle sensor for auto mode.

notes: Size by the room: aim for a unit rated well above your room's area so it cleans on its quiet speeds — an undersized purifier on max is a loud purifier that loses.
"True HEPA" is the phrase that matters; "HEPA-type" filters are not the same thing.
The real cost is filters — price a year of replacements before choosing, and stock a spare set before smoke season.
During renovations in pre-1990 homes, a purifier is a supplement to containment and HEPA vacuuming, never a substitute — see the lead and asbestos guides.

categories.name: Carbon monoxide alarms
categories.short: CSA-certified alarms — required by Ontario law near sleeping areas in homes with fuel appliances.
categories.why: If your home burns anything — gas, oil, propane, wood — or has an attached garage, Ontario law requires CO alarms adjacent to sleeping areas. They're $40–$80, they expire on a printed date, and they're the last line of defence behind the annual servicing and the audit's spillage check.

picks.name: First Alert CO615
picks.why: Plugs into any outlet with battery backup and shows the actual ppm reading — the display turns a mystery chirp into information.
picks.q: First Alert CO615 carbon monoxide alarm plug in

picks.name: Kidde Nighthawk (digital display)
picks.why: The long-running Kidde equivalent — AC powered, battery backup, digital readout, and a peak-level memory button that tells you what happened while you were out.
picks.q: Kidde Nighthawk carbon monoxide alarm digital display

picks.name: First Alert combination smoke + CO
picks.why: Where a smoke alarm is due for replacement anyway, a combination unit covers both requirements in one ceiling spot — check it carries both CSA marks.
picks.q: First Alert combination smoke carbon monoxide alarm Canada

notes: Look for CSA 6.19 certification — it's the Canadian standard CO alarms are tested to.
Every CO alarm has an end-of-life date printed on the back, typically 7–10 years from manufacture. Check yours today; replace on schedule.
One adjacent to each sleeping area is the legal minimum — one per storey with fuel appliances is the sensible spec.
An alarm is the backstop, not the fix: annual appliance servicing and the audit's combustion spillage check come first.

categories.name: Dehumidifiers & hygrometers
categories.short: Measure the moisture first ($20), then knock summer basement humidity down to the 30–50% band.
categories.why: Half of Ontario's musty-basement problem is seasonal: warm humid summer air meeting cool foundation walls. A $20 hygrometer proves whether you have a humidity problem at all; a properly sized dehumidifier fixes the summer half. The winter half — condensation on cold surfaces — is an insulation and ventilation problem the audit diagnoses, and no dehumidifier fixes it.

picks.name: Govee hygrometer (2-pack)
picks.why: Bluetooth-logging thermo-hygrometers for about $30 a pair — one upstairs, one in the basement, and a week of data tells you whether you need a dehumidifier at all.

picks.name: Midea Cube (35–50 pint)
picks.why: Compact footprint that nests for storage, app control, and a washable filter — sized right for typical basements at the 35-pint mark.

picks.name: hOmeLabs 50-pint
picks.why: The straightforward high-capacity unit for large or wet basements — pair it with its drain-hose outlet so you never empty a bucket.

notes: Winter indoor target is roughly 30–50% relative humidity; summer basements drift far above it without help.
Buy Energy Star and use the drain hose — the bucket is how dehumidifiers end up unplugged by November.
If humidity is fine but a cold corner still grows mould, that's a cold-surface (insulation) problem — the audit's thermal scan finds it.
Persistent high humidity in a tightened house is the textbook case for an HRV — ask the planner.

categories.name: Water test kits
categories.short: Lab-grade mail-in panels and screening strips — after you've used Ontario's free bacterial testing.
categories.why: Start with what's free: Public Health Ontario tests private well samples for E. coli and total coliforms at no charge. Paid kits earn their keep on what the free test doesn't cover — nitrates, metals like lead and arsenic, hardness, and city-water questions like lead service lines in pre-1960 neighbourhoods.

picks.name: Tap Score mail-in lab panel
picks.why: Mail-in kits analyzed at accredited labs with a readable report — choose the well panel (nitrates, metals, minerals) or the city panel (lead, chlorine by-products). The serious option when you need numbers you'd act on.

picks.name: Health Metric well water kit
picks.why: DIY strips for nitrate/nitrite, hardness, pH, iron and a bacteria presence test — a between-lab-tests screen, not a substitute for one.
picks.q: Health Metric well water test kit

picks.name: Safe Home lead-in-water test
picks.why: Lab-verified single-issue kit for the pre-1960 city-home question: is there lead in this tap's water? Worth running on any older home with original plumbing.
picks.q: Safe Home lead in drinking water test kit

notes: Ontario well owners: bacteriological testing is free through Public Health Ontario — never pay for what the public lab does better.
A TDS meter is not a safety test — it reads dissolved minerals, and dangerous water can score "clean". Skip it.
Test wells for chemistry when you move in, every few years after, and whenever taste, colour, or smell changes.
Keep every report — a documented water history matters at resale.
